lecture_title: 1.1 - Why Most Engineers Stop at the Surface
text: Welcome to Product Engineering Essentials. I'm glad you're here, and I want to start with a question that has nothing to do with syntax. Why do some developers, after three or four years of writing code, still feel stuck at the same level? They know the framework, they can ship a ticket, but the moment something behaves strangely, they're lost. My claim in this course is that the gap between a developer and a product engineer isn't syntax. It's knowing why the language behaves the way it does, and how code actually reaches users. Over the next eighteen lectures we'll close that gap together. And we won't do it with slides alone. We'll carry one running project the whole way through, so everything we learn lands in real code that you can open and run yourself.

lecture_title: 1.1 - Why Most Engineers Stop at the Surface
text: So what is the project? It's a link-preview widget. You know the thing: you paste a URL into a chat box or a social post, and a small card appears with a title, a description and a thumbnail image. Looks simple, right? But underneath there's a surprising amount of engineering. You have to fetch a page you don't control, parse messy HTML, pull out metadata like the Open Graph tags, cache the result so you don't hammer the same site, render a card, and handle every failure that the internet can throw at you. In this course we'll design that widget from first principles, build it using the patterns we learn, then review it, profile it and ship it to production. By the end, you'll have a folder called link-preview with a real, working widget inside.

lecture_title: 1.1 - Why Most Engineers Stop at the Surface
text: Let me tell you how the course is laid out, so you know where we're heading. First we have the engineer's mindset: first principles, and how to read specs and source code instead of waiting for a blog post. Then we rebuild JavaScript's architecture from JS 1.0, through prototypes, and we'll see why so many strange behaviours are actually historical decisions. After that comes asynchronous JavaScript, where we'll look at the event loop and the microtask queue, because our widget fetches pages and has to wait. Then functional patterns: pure functions, composition and closures, which we'll use to structure the widget's code. And finally production engineering, meaning code review, performance profiling, and shipping from a pull request to real users. Each chapter feeds the same project, so nothing is wasted.

lecture_title: 1.1 - Why Most Engineers Stop at the Surface
text: A quick word on how to get the most out of this. Don't just watch. When I open a file, open it with me. When I say pause and try, genuinely pause. The point isn't that you remember my code, it's that you build the habit of asking why before you ask how. We'll also stay honest about trade-offs. Almost nothing in engineering is simply right or wrong, it's right for a context. So I'll keep saying things like, what does this cost us, and who pays for it. For this first chapter we'll stay mostly conceptual, but I promise code is coming. In the very next lecture we'll look at why most engineers stop at the surface, and what it takes to go one level deeper. Okay? Let's get started.

Let's start with a question that sounds almost silly. Why do most engineers stop at the surface? I don't think it's laziness. I think it's incentives. When you're new, the fastest way to be useful is to copy a pattern that works. You search for how to fetch data in JavaScript, you paste the snippet, the card shows up, and the ticket is closed. That's a perfectly rational thing to do. The trouble is that it builds a layer of knowledge that has no floor beneath it. You know what to type, but not what happens when you type it. And the day the snippet doesn't work, you have nothing to reason from. You can only search again and hope someone had the same problem.

Let me make this concrete with our link-preview widget. Imagine a teammate writes `const res = await fetch(url)` and then `const html = await res.text()`, and it works in the demo. Great. Then in production, a handful of links just hang the UI. A surface-level engineer says, fetch is flaky. A product engineer asks different questions. Does fetch have a timeout by default? Where is that request waiting, in the browser or on the server? What happens to the promise while it waits? Is something blocking the main thread, or is the thread free and we just never get an answer? Notice that none of these questions are about syntax. They're about the machine underneath the syntax, and they're the questions this course will teach you to ask.

So how do you go below the surface without drowning? My rule is to go exactly one level down, every time something surprises you. If a function behaves unexpectedly, don't just patch the symptom. Ask what that function is actually made of. If a framework does magic, ask what the plain version would look like. Take our widget: before we reach for any library to parse HTML, we'll ask what parsing even means, and what a browser does when it receives a string of tags. One level down is cheap. It costs you ten or fifteen minutes. But across a year, those fifteen minute detours turn into a mental model, and the mental model is what separates people who debug in minutes from people who debug in days.

There's one more reason engineers stay on the surface, and it's fear. Reading the specification feels like homework, and reading source code feels like walking into someone else's house. I want to remove that fear, because it's mostly unfounded. Specs are written in a very regular style, and source code is just code. You've been reading code your whole career. So here's the deal for this chapter. Next lecture we'll learn first principles thinking, which is the method. And in the lecture after that, we'll use the method by reading real specs and real source. By the end of chapter one, you won't need anyone's permission to look under the hood. You'll just do it, and you'll enjoy it more than you expect.

First principles thinking. This phrase gets thrown around a lot, so let me define it in a practical way. A first principle is something you can't break down any further without leaving the problem. Everything above it is built from it. So thinking from first principles means that instead of reasoning by analogy, which is, other people do it this way so I will too, you break the problem down to what must be true, and build up from there. It's slower at the start. But it gives you something analogy never can: the ability to handle a situation nobody has written a tutorial for. And honestly, that's most of real product work. Your situation is almost never exactly like the example in the documentation.

Let's apply it to our widget before we write any code. Question one: what is a link preview, at its core? Strip away the card and the styling. It's a function that takes a URL and returns a small object of metadata, a title, a description, an image, and maybe a site name. That's it. So the first principle is, `url` in, `{ title, description, image }` out. Question two: where does that information live? On the target page, inside meta tags in the head of the HTML. Question three: who is allowed to read it? Here the browser's rules about cross-origin requests will matter a lot, which means a browser can't always fetch the page directly. See how much design we've done without typing a line? The decisions fell out of the principles.

Now let's turn that into a tiny design. Since the browser may not be allowed to read another site's HTML, our widget will call a small endpoint that we control, and that endpoint will do the fetching. So we get two pieces. A server-side function, which I'll call `fetchPreview`, that downloads the page and extracts metadata. And a client-side function called `createLinkPreview` that asks our endpoint and renders the card. I'm deliberately not naming any framework. If tomorrow we change from one server framework to another, these two responsibilities stay exactly the same. That's a good sign. When your design follows from principles rather than tools, it survives when the tools change, which they always do.

Let me give you a checklist you can reuse, and I'll say it as plain sentences rather than a slide. When you face a new problem, first write down the input and the output in one line. Second, list what must be true for the output to be correct. Third, separate what you know from what you're assuming, and be honest about the assumptions, because those are where bugs hide. Fourth, find the smallest experiment that tests one assumption. Notice that the fourth step is the bridge to our next lecture. How do you test an assumption about how fetch, or HTML parsing, or the browser actually works? You read the specification, and you read the source. That's where the truth lives, and that's what we'll do next.

Welcome to chapter two, JavaScript architecture. In this lecture I want to give you a mental model I call the wave model of JavaScript. The idea is that JavaScript didn't arrive as one finished language. It arrived in waves, and each wave added features to solve the problems of its era, while carefully keeping everything from the previous waves working. If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember that. The language you write today is layers of sediment, and many of its oddities are simply the edges where one wave met another. Understanding the waves turns confusing behaviour into history that you can reason about.

Let me sketch the waves, roughly. Wave one, in the nineties, is JavaScript as a small scripting language for making web pages react to clicks. Wave two is the period around ECMAScript 3, when browsers competed and the language spread everywhere, along with the pain of cross-browser differences. Wave three is the long pause and then ES5, which brought strict mode and methods like `map` and `filter`. Wave four is ES2015, often called ES6, which was huge: classes, modules, arrow functions, promises, `let` and `const`. And wave five is the yearly cadence since then, with small steady additions like `async` and `await`, optional chaining and more. Each wave has a flavour, and you can often tell which wave a piece of code comes from just by reading it.

Why does this matter for our link-preview widget? Because the code we write will touch several waves at once. Our `fetchPreview` function will use `async` and `await`, a recent wave. But the HTML it parses was written for the oldest waves, with missing quotes and unclosed tags, and the browser's parsing rules are designed to be forgiving in the same way early JavaScript was. And our helper that merges options might use a pattern from a more recent wave, `Object.assign`, which arrived with ES2015. Neither is wrong. They're just different eras living in one file. When you can name the era, you can predict the behaviour, and you know which assumptions are safe.

The big principle behind all the waves is backward compatibility, and it's worth saying out loud, because it's what makes JavaScript different from most languages. The web has a rule, sometimes phrased as, don't break the web. If a page worked in 1999, the committee tries very hard to ensure it still works. So mistakes are rarely fixed. They're worked around, by adding new features beside the old ones. That's why we have both `var` and `let`, both functions and arrow functions. In the next lecture we'll go to the very beginning, wave one, and look at how JavaScript 1.0 was designed, and which of its decisions we're still living with today.

Before we move on, try a small exercise. Open any JavaScript file you wrote recently and pick three lines. For each one, guess which wave it belongs to: the nineties, ES5, or ES2015 and later. You'll be surprised how quickly you start seeing the layers, and how much it helps.

Now we go back to the beginning. How was JavaScript 1.0 designed? The short, famous story is that Brendan Eich created the first version at Netscape in May 1995, in about ten days. It was first called Mocha, then LiveScript, and then JavaScript, a name chosen largely for marketing because Java was popular at the time. But the language has nothing to do with Java beyond some syntax. And I want to push back on the idea that ten days means it was sloppy. It means the design was small, and the constraints were extremely clear. Constraints are a gift, and understanding them explains almost everything strange in the language.

What were the constraints? First, it had to look familiar to people who knew Java and C, so it got curly braces, `if`, `for` and semicolons. Second, it had to be approachable for designers and people who weren't professional programmers, so it got loose typing and automatic conversions. Third, it was meant to be a glue language running inside the browser, handling events like clicks, so functions needed to be easy to pass around. And inspired by a language called Scheme, JavaScript made functions first-class values. And the object system was inspired by a language called Self, which uses prototypes instead of classes. A C-like face, a Scheme-like heart, and a Self-like object model. That's the recipe.

Let's see these decisions at work in our widget's code. Loose typing and automatic conversion is why `'5' + 1` gives `'51'` but `'5' - 1` gives `4`. When our `parseMetadata` function reads a width attribute from an image tag, it gets a string, and if we're careless the arithmetic goes wrong. First-class functions is why we can pass a handler into `createLinkPreview(url, onReady)` without any ceremony. And the prototype heritage is why our preview card object can share methods without a class keyword. Every one of these is a direct line from a 1995 design decision to a bug or a feature in a file we'll write this week. I think that's pretty remarkable.

Let me close with a fair assessment. Some of those early choices were genuinely regrettable, like the `==` operator's coercion rules, and the way `this` changes depending on how a function is called. But many were brilliant, and are the reason JavaScript could grow so far. First-class functions, closures and flexible objects are exactly what let us build rich things with so little syntax. The right takeaway isn't, the language is bad. It's that every feature is an answer to a question someone asked in a particular year. In the next lecture we'll follow the language forward and ask why it evolved the way it did, and why it's still evolving today.

One small exercise before the next lecture. Open your browser console and type `typeof null`, then `'5' - 1`, then `'5' + 1`. Each answer is a fossil from 1995. Write down which design constraint explains each one, and we'll compare notes.

So JavaScript 1.0 was small and quick. Why did it evolve into what we have today, and why in this specific way? There are two forces I want you to see. The first is competition, and the second is governance. In the late nineties, Netscape and Microsoft each shipped their own versions with their own features, and developers suffered. The answer was standardization. The language was handed to a standards body called Ecma International, and that's why the official name is ECMAScript. JavaScript is the common name, ECMAScript is the standard. When you hear ES5 or ES2015, those are editions of the standard, and the browsers implement them.

The second force is a process. Today new features are proposed to a committee called TC39, and each proposal moves through numbered stages, from stage zero, an idea, up to stage four, which means it's finished and will be in the next edition. A feature needs at least two real implementations and tests before it gets there. That's very deliberate, because of the rule we discussed: once a feature ships on the web, it basically can never be removed. So the committee moves carefully. When you see something like optional chaining, `user?.profile?.name`, you're looking at the output of that slow, careful pipeline. And you can read every proposal on GitHub, which is a great exercise in reading primary sources.

Now let's make this useful. Because of that process, we can write modern code and still support older environments, using tools called transpilers and polyfills. A transpiler such as Babel rewrites new syntax into old syntax. A polyfill adds a missing function, like `Promise`, using old code. For our widget, we have to decide our support target. Do we ship `async` and `await` straight to the browser, or compile it down? That's a product decision, not a technical one. It depends on who our users are. If your analytics say that nearly everyone uses a modern browser, shipping modern code means smaller bundles and faster loads, and we'll come back to that when we profile.

So here's what I want you to take from this chapter. JavaScript's strangeness is explained by its history: a fast start, heavy competition, standardization, and then a careful, backward compatible evolution. With this model, you stop being surprised and start predicting. Next chapter we apply it to the part of the language that confuses people the most, and that is prototypes. We'll open up the hidden `[[Prototype]]` link, see how objects find their properties, and later use it to build the shared methods of our link-preview card. It's the biggest idea from wave one, so it deserves a full chapter.

If you have time, open the TC39 proposals repository on GitHub and read the README of one finished proposal. Notice how much of it is motivation and trade-offs rather than syntax. That habit of reading the reasoning is exactly what we're practicing here.

Welcome to chapter three, prototypes and inheritance. In this first lecture we look under the hood at something written as double square brackets, `[[Prototype]]`. That notation comes straight from the specification, and it means an internal slot. It's a hidden property that every object has, and you can't access it with a normal dot. It points either to another object or to `null`. That's the whole idea. Every object can have a link to another object, and when you ask for a property that the first object doesn't have, JavaScript quietly goes and asks the linked one. Everything else in this chapter, classes included, is built on that one link, so let's make it real with code, okay?

Open a file called prototype-demo.js in our link-preview folder. I'll write `const base = { kind: 'link' }`, and then `const card = Object.create(base)`. The function `Object.create` makes a brand new empty object and sets its `[[Prototype]]` to whatever we pass in. Now if I log `card.kind`, I get `'link'`, even though `card` itself has no property called kind. Let me prove that with `Object.hasOwn(card, 'kind')`, which returns `false`. So the value was found on the linked object. And to see the hidden link directly, there's `Object.getPrototypeOf(card)`, which returns `base`. You'll also see an old accessor named `__proto__` in legacy code, but prefer the function forms, since they're the standard, supported way.

Now what happens when we write instead of read? If I say `card.title = 'Hello'`, JavaScript creates the property on `card` itself, not on `base`. That's called shadowing when the same name exists further up. The prototype is never modified by writes to the child. This is a super important fact, and it's the reason that sharing through prototypes is safe for methods but dangerous for shared mutable data. Suppose `base` had an array called `tags`, and we do `card.tags.push('news')`. We aren't assigning, we're reading `tags` through the chain, and mutating the shared array, so every object linked to `base` sees the change. I've seen that bug in production more than once, and it's a great interview question as well.

So how does this connect to our widget? We want many preview card objects, each with their own data, but sharing the same behaviour, like `render` and `destroy`. With prototypes, we create a single object, `cardMethods`, that holds those functions, and each card is made with `Object.create(cardMethods)`. Memory is saved because the functions exist once. The data, like the title and image, lives on each card as own properties. That's the pattern, and we'll write it for real shortly. But first, in the next lecture, we'll visualize the full chain, because `base` has its own prototype too, and that's how `toString` shows up on everything.

Last time we saw that an object can link to another object. Today we visualize the whole prototype chain, because links can be followed repeatedly. When you read `card.toString`, JavaScript looks at `card`, doesn't find it, follows the link to `base`, doesn't find it, follows the link again to `Object.prototype`, and finds `toString` there. And `Object.prototype` has a `[[Prototype]]` of `null`, and that's the end of the chain. So the lookup rule is a loop: check own properties, move to the prototype, repeat until found or until null. If it reaches null, you get `undefined`. That's the entire algorithm for property lookup, and it's literally written like that in the specification, in an operation called OrdinaryGet.

Let me draw it in the console. I'll create `function Preview(url) { this.url = url }`, and then add a method with `Preview.prototype.render = function () { return this.url }`. Now `const p = new Preview('https://example.com')`. Three things are happening. First, every function has a property called `prototype`, which is a plain object. Second, when we call a function with `new`, JavaScript creates an empty object and links its `[[Prototype]]` to that `prototype` object. Third, it runs the function body with `this` pointing at the new object. Check it yourself: `Object.getPrototypeOf(p) === Preview.prototype` is `true`. People mix up `prototype` and `[[Prototype]]` constantly. One belongs to functions, the other belongs to every object.

Now the chain for `p` goes like this. `p` itself has the own property `url`. Its link goes to `Preview.prototype`, which has `render` and a property called `constructor`. Its link goes to `Object.prototype`, which has `toString`, `hasOwnProperty` and friends. Then `null`. If I call `p.render()`, it's found on the second link. If I call `p.toString()`, it's found on the third. And arrays work the same way: an array's chain goes to `Array.prototype`, which holds `map` and `filter`, then to `Object.prototype`. That's how `[].map` exists without every array carrying its own copy. This is also what the `class` keyword sits on top of. A class is, underneath, a function with a prototype object. Same machinery, nicer clothes.

Let's use this knowledge to debug something. Suppose in our widget someone loops over a card with `for (const key in card)` and finds a method name appearing in the output that they never set. Why? Because `for...in` walks the chain too, and lists enumerable properties it inherits. The fix is to check `Object.hasOwn(card, key)` or to use `Object.keys(card)`, which only returns own properties. This is the sort of bug that disappears the moment you hold the chain picture in your head. In the next lecture, we get a bit mischievous. We'll hack the prototype on purpose, and then talk about when that's a brilliant move and when it's a terrible one.

Time to hack the prototype. Since a prototype is just an ordinary object, we can change it at runtime, and every object linked to it sees the change instantly, even ones created earlier. Let me show you. Take `Preview.prototype` from last time. I'll add `Preview.prototype.host = function () { return new URL(this.url).hostname }`. And now `p.host()` works, even though `p` was created before we wrote that method. The lookup happens at the moment of the call, walking the chain fresh. This live linking is powerful, because you can add behaviour late, patch bugs in objects you didn't create, and build plugin systems with very little code.

Now the dangerous version: modifying built-ins. You can write `Array.prototype.last = function () { return this[this.length - 1] }`, and suddenly every array in the program has a `last` method. This is called monkey patching. It's tempting, and in the early days of the web, libraries did it all the time. One famous library extended built-in prototypes, and when the language later added its own method with the same name but different behaviour, pages broke. That's actually why a method called `flatten` ended up named `flat`, and one named `contains` became `includes`. The committee worked around existing patches. So the rule: never patch built-ins in shared code, because you're editing a global that every library depends on.

There are legitimate uses, though. A polyfill is a controlled patch: you check first with `if (!Array.prototype.at) { ... }` and only then add it, matching the specification exactly. And in tests, you might temporarily replace a method on an object to fake a network call, then restore it. For our widget, let me use a safe, local hack. I'll create `const cardMethods = { render() {...}, destroy() {...} }`, and a factory, `function makeCard(data) { return Object.assign(Object.create(cardMethods), data) }`. Now if a special card type, say a video preview, needs a different `render`, we make `videoMethods = Object.create(cardMethods)` and override only `render`. Method overriding by chain order, with no classes in sight.

Let me add two safety tools you should know. `Object.freeze(Preview.prototype)` stops anyone from changing it afterward, which is useful for library code. And `Object.setPrototypeOf` can change an existing object's link, but engines like V8 optimize objects based on their shape, and changing the prototype after creation can slow them down, so prefer `Object.create` at the start. That's a nice bridge to performance, which we'll profile properly in chapter six. For now, you understand the object model. Next chapter, we apply our first principles to asynchronous JavaScript, because our widget has to wait for the network, and to understand waiting, we need the event loop.

Chapter four, asynchronous JavaScript, and we begin with the event loop from first principles. Let's start with a fact that surprises many people. JavaScript, the language, can do one thing at a time. A single thread runs your code, one function after another, using a structure called the call stack. When you call a function, it's pushed onto the stack. When it returns, it's popped. If a function takes a long time, nothing else can happen: no clicks, no rendering, no timers. That sounds like a terrible design for a language that needs to wait for networks. So how does our widget wait for a page to download without freezing the browser? The answer is that the waiting isn't done by JavaScript.

The waiting is done by the environment around JavaScript, the browser or Node, which has its own components written in languages like C++. When our code calls `fetch(url)`, JavaScript hands the request to the browser and immediately continues. The browser does the network work on its own threads. When the response arrives, the browser needs a way to run our callback, but it can't just interrupt whatever is running. So it places a task in a queue, called the task queue, or sometimes the macrotask queue. And then there's the event loop, which is a simple loop with a very clear job: when the call stack is empty, take the next task from the queue and push it onto the stack. That's it. That's the whole idea.

Let's watch it happen. In a file, I'll write `console.log('A')`, then `setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0)`, then `console.log('C')`. What order do we see? A, C, B. Even with a delay of zero. Why? Because `setTimeout` hands the callback to the browser's timer, and the timer, once it expires, queues a task. But our script is still running on the stack, and the loop only picks a new task when the stack is empty. So `C` prints first. The zero doesn't mean now, it means as soon as possible after the current work. Keep this example in mind, because everything in this chapter, promises and async await included, is a variation on it.

Here's why this matters in our widget. Imagine that after fetching a page, we parse it with a big synchronous loop that takes two hundred milliseconds. During those two hundred milliseconds, the stack is busy, so the loop can't run anything else. The page can't repaint, so animations stutter and clicks feel dead. That's the classic main thread problem. So the design rule is: keep each task short, and break up long work. In the next lecture we'll look at how callbacks, promises and async await let us express waiting in code, and what each one is doing with this loop behind the scenes.

In the last lecture we saw that the browser queues a callback when work finishes. The simplest way to express that is a callback function, and that's where asynchronous JavaScript began. In our widget, imagine `fetchPreview(url, callback)`, where the callback receives an error and a result. It works, but it gets ugly when steps depend on each other. First fetch the page, then parse it, then fetch the image to check its size, then save to the cache. Each step nests inside the previous one, and every level needs its own error handling. People call this callback hell, but the real problem isn't the indentation. It's that control flow and errors are scattered and easy to lose. We needed a better value to represent a future result.

That value is the promise. A promise is an object representing the eventual result of an operation, and it's always in one of three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. Once it settles, it never changes again. You attach handlers with `.then` and `.catch`, and `.then` returns a new promise, which is why you can chain them. So `fetch(url).then(res => res.text()).then(html => parseMetadata(html))` reads top to bottom, and a single `.catch` at the end handles an error from any step. Notice that we're still using the loop we know: when a promise settles, its handlers are scheduled to run later, not immediately, even if the promise was already resolved. That guarantee, that handlers always run asynchronously, makes behaviour predictable.

Now async await. It's syntax on top of promises, not a new mechanism. I'll write `async function fetchPreview(url) { const res = await fetch(url); const html = await res.text(); return parseMetadata(html) }`. An async function always returns a promise. And `await` pauses that function, only that function, until the awaited promise settles, then continues. While paused, the call stack is free, so the browser keeps running everything else. Under the hood, the engine turns the function into something like a state machine: each await is a point where it can suspend and later resume. Errors become ordinary exceptions, so we can use `try` and `catch`. Same power as promises, but it reads like synchronous code, which is why we'll use it in the widget.

A couple of traps to avoid. First, `await` inside a loop makes things sequential. If our widget previews five links, `for (const url of urls) { await fetchPreview(url) }` runs them one at a time. For parallel work, we start them all and wait together with `await Promise.all(urls.map(fetchPreview))`. Second, forgetting to `await` gives you a promise instead of a value, and failures become unhandled rejections that surface late, or never. Third, `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one fails, so for a list of links where some may be broken, use `Promise.allSettled`, so the good previews still render. Next lecture, we zoom into the part of the event loop that makes promises special: the microtask queue.

We left a mystery last time: promise handlers are asynchronous, but are they in the same queue as `setTimeout` callbacks? They're not. Besides the task queue, there's a second queue called the microtask queue, and it has higher priority. After each task finishes, and the call stack is empty, the engine drains the entire microtask queue before it moves on to the next task or lets the browser render. Promise handlers and `queueMicrotask` callbacks go into the microtask queue. Timers, clicks, and network events go into the task queue. So the more precise event loop is: run one task, then run all microtasks until the queue is empty, then maybe render, then take the next task.

Let's test our understanding with a puzzle. Write `console.log('1')`, then `setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0)`, then `Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'))`, then `console.log('4')`. What's the output? Walk through it. The script itself is the first task, so `1` prints, the timer is registered, the promise handler goes to the microtask queue, and `4` prints. The script ends, the stack is empty, and the engine drains microtasks, so `3` prints. Only then the next task, the timer, runs and prints `2`. So the answer is 1, 4, 3, 2. If you got that right, you understand more than many people who've used promises for years. Pause the video, and try making up your own variation.

There's a subtle consequence: microtasks can starve the loop. If a microtask schedules another microtask, and that schedules another, the queue never empties, so the engine never reaches the next task, and the page can't render. An infinite promise chain freezes the tab just like a `while(true)` loop. So in our widget, if we process a long list of previews by chaining thousands of tiny promise steps, the UI would hang until all of them finish. The cure is to yield to the task queue now and then, for example by awaiting a small `setTimeout` wrapper, so the browser gets a chance to paint between batches. Microtasks are for finishing the current job promptly, not for long running work.

Let's apply this to the widget's rendering. When the metadata arrives, we call `renderCard`, and we want the card to appear and fade in. If we add the element and set the class in the same microtask run, the browser never paints the starting state, so no transition happens. The fix is to wait a frame with `requestAnimationFrame`, which runs before the next paint. So you can see why the model matters: it tells you exactly when your code runs relative to painting. That wraps up asynchronous JavaScript. In chapter five we shift gears into functional programming, where we'll make the widget's core logic predictable and testable with pure functions.

Welcome to chapter five, functional programming patterns. We start with pure functions and immutability, because they're the easiest way to make code predictable. A pure function has two properties. First, given the same arguments, it always returns the same result. Second, it has no side effects: it doesn't change anything outside itself, it doesn't write to a variable somewhere else, it doesn't log, it doesn't touch the network. Why do we care? Because a pure function can be understood by reading it alone. You don't need to know the state of the world. You can test it with one line, and you can call it twice without fear. In our link-preview widget, the messy parts, the network and the DOM, will be small and pushed to the edges.

Let's find the pure core of our widget. Consider `parseMetadata(html)`. It takes a string and returns `{ title, description, image }`. It doesn't fetch anything and doesn't touch the page. Same input, same output, so it's pure, and testing it is trivial: pass a small HTML string with an `og:title` tag and check the result. Compare that with a version that reads from `document.querySelector` and writes straight into the card. That one depends on the current page and changes it, so you can't test it without a browser. By splitting `fetchPreview`, which is impure because it performs a network call, from `parseMetadata`, which is pure, we keep the part with the most logic easy to verify.

Now immutability. Mutating data, like `card.title = 'New'`, is a side effect that other code holding the same object might not expect. The immutable alternative is to create a new object with the change. I'll write `const next = { ...card, title: 'New' }`. The spread operator copies the own enumerable properties into a fresh object, and the later property wins. For arrays, instead of `push`, we use `[...items, item]`, or `map` and `filter`, which return new arrays. Be aware that spread is shallow: nested objects are still shared. So if `card.image` is an object and we change `next.image.width`, we've also changed `card.image`. For nested updates, we copy each level that changes, and leave the rest alone.

Is immutability free? No, and I want to be honest about it. Copying costs time and memory, and for huge data structures it adds up, which is why libraries like Immer and persistent data structures exist. For our widget, with small objects, the cost is negligible and the benefit is large: we can keep a history of previews, compare old and new by reference, and never wonder who changed what. You can also enforce it during development with `Object.freeze`, which makes writes fail in strict mode. Next lecture we'll take these small pure functions and glue them together with function composition, which will turn our fetching and parsing steps into a clean pipeline.

Function composition is the idea that you build bigger behaviour by chaining small functions, where the output of one becomes the input of the next. In math, you may have seen f of g of x. In JavaScript, it's `f(g(x))`. That's already composition. The value comes when each function does one thing, takes one argument and returns one result, so they fit together like pipes. Our link-preview widget is a natural pipeline: take a URL, normalize it, fetch the HTML, extract the metadata, clean the text, and produce the card data. Each of those steps can be a tiny function. And if each step is pure, or we deal with the impure one separately, the pipeline is easy to reason about.

Let me write a helper. `const pipe = (...fns) => (input) => fns.reduce((acc, fn) => fn(acc), input)`. Read it slowly. `pipe` takes any number of functions and returns a new function. That new function takes an input and uses `reduce` to feed it through the functions left to right, passing the accumulated result along. Now our synchronous steps become: `const toCardData = pipe(extractTags, pickBestFields, cleanText, truncate)`. I like how that reads like a sentence. Each of those four functions is a few lines, and we can test them one at a time. If you prefer right-to-left, as in mathematics, you'd name it `compose` and use `reduceRight`. Same idea, the order is the only difference.

Composition works best when functions have the same shape, and that's where partial application and currying help. Say `truncate` needs a maximum length and the text. I'd write `const truncate = (max) => (text) => text.length > max ? text.slice(0, max - 1) + '…' : text`. Now `truncate(120)` is a function waiting for the text, perfect for the pipeline: `pipe(cleanText, truncate(120))`. We've configured it in advance, and what's left takes one argument. This is a closure at work, since the inner function remembers `max`, and we'll look at closures properly in the next lecture. Notice that we didn't need classes, inheritance, or any framework. Just functions that return functions.

What about asynchronous steps? A promise breaks the simple pipe, because the output is a promise, not a value. The fix is an async version: `const pipeAsync = (...fns) => (input) => fns.reduce((acc, fn) => acc.then(fn), Promise.resolve(input))`. Each step is awaited before the next. So `pipeAsync(normalizeUrl, fetchHtml, toCardData)` handles the whole flow, and `fetchHtml` can be async while the rest stay synchronous, since `.then` accepts either. One warning: debugging a long pipeline can be hard, because errors surface at the end. A tiny helper that logs a value and passes it along, often called `tap`, lets you peek in the middle without breaking the chain.

Closures as state. We've already used closures twice without naming them, so let's name them now. A closure is a function together with the variables from the place where it was created. When a function is defined inside another, it can keep using the outer function's variables, even after the outer function has returned. This works because JavaScript functions carry a reference to their lexical environment, the scope they were born in. Nobody else can reach those variables, only that function. So a closure gives you private, persistent state without a class and without a global. That's a powerful combination, and it's the basis of caching, memoization, and many module patterns.

Let's build the cache for our widget. I'll write `function createPreviewCache(ttlMs) { const store = new Map(); return { get(url) {...}, set(url, data) {...} } }`. The `store` variable lives inside `createPreviewCache`. After the function returns, the only way to touch `store` is through `get` and `set`. In `set`, I write `store.set(url, { data, expires: Date.now() + ttlMs })`. In `get`, I read the entry, and if `Date.now()` is past `expires`, I delete it and return `undefined`. So we have a small stateful object, a time to live cache, with a private map. Multiple caches don't interfere, since each call creates a new `store`. Compare that with a global `previewCache` object, which any file could modify.

Now memoization, which is caching at the level of a function. `const memoize = (fn) => { const seen = new Map(); return (arg) => { if (!seen.has(arg)) seen.set(arg, fn(arg)); return seen.get(arg) } }`. We wrap a pure function like `parseMetadata` so that repeated calls with the same HTML string return the stored result. This is exactly why purity matters: memoization is only safe for functions whose output depends only on the input. For `fetchPreview`, we memoize the promise rather than the value, `seen.set(url, fetchPreview(url))`, so that two components asking for the same link at the same moment share one request. That's a real, practical optimization in link-heavy feeds.

Let me warn you about the classic closure bug, because it's an interview favorite. Using `var` in a loop, `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i)) }` prints three, three, three, since all callbacks share the same single `i`. With `let`, each iteration gets its own binding, so it prints zero, one, two. Also remember that closures keep their variables alive, so a cache that never evicts entries is a memory leak, which is why our cache has a time limit. Great, that completes the functional patterns. Now our widget has pure parsing, a pipeline and a cache, and chapter six asks the question every real project faces: is this good enough to ship?

Welcome to the last chapter, production engineering. We have a working link-preview widget. Now we ask: would you trust it with real users? The first practice is code review. And I want to start with why. Review isn't there to catch typos, tools do that. Review exists to spread knowledge, to catch design mistakes while they're cheap to fix, and to make sure at least two people understand every line that ships. A bug found in review costs minutes. The same bug found by a user costs trust. And culture matters more than process. If review feels like an exam, people hide their work. If it feels like collaboration, people share early, and the code gets better.

Let's review our own widget as an author first. Before opening a pull request, read your own diff as if a stranger wrote it. Is the change small enough to understand in fifteen or twenty minutes? If it touches the cache, the fetcher and the card rendering together, split it. Does the description explain why, not just what? I'd write: this adds a timeout to `fetchPreview` because some sites never respond, which freezes the loading state. Did you add a test for `parseMetadata` with a page that has no Open Graph tags? Authors who do this make reviewers' jobs easy, and reviewers who feel respected give much better feedback in return.

Now as a reviewer, here's what I look for, in order. First, correctness: does it do what the description says, and what happens with empty, huge or malicious input? For our widget, the biggest one is security. If we fetch any URL a user gives us on the server, someone can ask us to fetch internal addresses, like a cloud metadata endpoint. That's called server-side request forgery, and we must block private IP ranges. And when rendering the title, set `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, since page metadata is untrusted. Second, design: is it simple, are names clear, are the responsibilities separated? Third, tests. Last, style, which should be automated. Ordering matters, because arguing about semicolons while missing an SSRF hole is the wrong priority.

Tone is part of the review. Ask questions instead of issuing orders: what happens if the response has no `content-type` header? Separate must fix from nice to have, with a prefix like nit. Praise good things too, it's not fluff, it tells people what to repeat. And as the author, don't take comments personally, and don't argue every point: either fix, or explain, and thank them. If a thread goes beyond three exchanges, talk face to face. One more habit: reviews should be fast. A pull request waiting two days blocks the author and makes the next change bigger. In the next lecture, we move from is it correct to is it fast, with performance profiling.

Performance profiling. The first rule is the one everyone breaks: don't guess, measure. Engineers are famously bad at predicting where time goes. I've watched people spend a week optimizing a loop that took two milliseconds, while a ten second wait for a network call went untouched. So profiling is a method. Define what slow means, in a number, measure it, find the biggest contributor, change one thing, and measure again. For our link-preview widget, what are the numbers? Probably the time from pasting a link to seeing the card, and the cost of rendering a feed with fifty cards. Let's open Chrome DevTools and look at real data rather than opinions.

Open the Performance panel, press record, paste a link into the widget, and stop the recording. You'll see a flame chart. The horizontal axis is time and each bar is a function call, with callees stacked underneath their callers. Wide bars are expensive. Look for long tasks, which DevTools marks with a red corner, those over fifty milliseconds, because they block the main thread, exactly as we discussed in the event loop lecture. In our recording, I see a wide bar under `parseMetadata`. We were parsing the html with a regular expression that backtracks badly on long pages. That's a real finding, and it came from the data, not from a hunch. We'll replace it with a proper parser that walks the head only.

The Network panel tells the other half of the story. Check the waterfall. Is our endpoint slow, or is it the target site? If the preview image is two megabytes, the card is waiting for pixels, so we should ask the server to return a resized thumbnail, and set `loading='lazy'` on the image element. And the Memory panel helps with leaks: take a heap snapshot, scroll through a long feed, take another, and compare. If detached DOM nodes keep growing, something, probably an event listener or our cache closure, is holding references. Remember the cache we wrote with a time limit? This is where we'd see if it works. Profile before and after each fix, and write the numbers in the pull request.

Let me give you a summary of what to optimize, in priority order. First, do less work: don't fetch what's cached, and don't render what's off screen. Second, do it later, defer non critical work, and split long tasks so the browser can paint. Third, do it in parallel, as we did with `Promise.all`. Only fourth, make the work itself faster by tuning code. Most wins come from the first two. And set a budget, like the card appears in under one second on a typical connection, and fail the build if it regresses. Now we have something correct, reviewed and fast enough. The final lecture is the one that matters most to the user: getting it out the door.

lecture_title: 6.3 - Ship It: From PR to Production
text: Ship it. From pull request to production, and then a wrap up of the whole course. A feature doesn't create value until it reaches users, and the path from a merged pull request to a running service should be boring, automated and reversible. The pipeline we want is called continuous integration and continuous delivery. On every pull request, a server runs the linter and the tests, including our `parseMetadata` tests, and builds the widget. If anything fails, the merge is blocked. After merge, the same pipeline builds an artifact and deploys it. The key word is same: you want the exact thing that you tested to be the thing that runs in production, not something rebuilt by hand.

lecture_title: 6.3 - Ship It: From PR to Production
text: Deployment strategy matters. For our link-preview endpoint, I'd deploy first to a staging environment that mimics production, run a smoke test that fetches a known page and checks the title, and then release gradually. A feature flag lets us merge code that's switched off, then turn it on for one percent of users, then ten, then everyone, and turn it off instantly if something misbehaves. Separating deploying from releasing is one of the most useful ideas in modern engineering. And always have a rollback plan you've actually tried: redeploy the previous version, or flip the flag. If rollback takes more than a few minutes, you aren't ready to ship.

lecture_title: 6.3 - Ship It: From PR to Production
text: Once it's live, you need to see it. Three things. Logs, structured ones, so that we can search by URL and status. Metrics, like the request rate, error rate and the ninety fifth percentile latency of `fetchPreview`. And alerts, which fire on symptoms users feel, such as the error rate staying above a threshold, rather than on every blip. For our widget, I'd also track the cache hit ratio, because it tells us whether the closure we built is paying off. And have a plain, short document, a runbook, explaining what to do when the alert fires at three in the morning. Shipping isn't the end of the work. It's where you start learning from real use.

lecture_title: 6.3 - Ship It: From PR to Production
text: Let's wrap up the course. We began by asking why many engineers stop at the surface, and answered it with first principles and a habit of reading specs and source. We rebuilt JavaScript through its waves, understood prototypes, the event loop and the microtask queue, and used functional patterns, pure functions, composition and closures, to shape the widget. Then we reviewed it, profiled it and shipped it. You now have a link-preview widget, but more importantly a way of working: ask why, go one level down, measure, and ship in small safe steps. Pick any part, extend it, maybe add support for oEmbed or a dark mode card, and apply these habits. Thank you for building with me, and I'll see you in the next course.
